agree.reason: The two commissioners focused on traffic get only an admission that the intersection drops to a D and a request to accept 'a slightly longer wait.' The speech never mentions the builder's offer to pay for a signal that keeps the intersection at C, and it never asks for that signal as a condition of approval, so they have little reason to change their vote.

honest.reason: The speech is mostly faithful to the facts and openly says traffic will get worse, but two lines go too far. 'Residents won't be pushing their cars out onto our street' claims more than 72 spaces for 64 units can guarantee, and the jobs listed for future residents are guesses presented as facts.

works_the_facts.reason: The figures are repeated as given and never worked into anything more useful, such as 64 homes housing about one in six of the 412 households on the waiting list, or 1.1 parking spaces per unit.

right_comparison.reason: It sets the project against the status quo of an empty lot and a three-year wait, which is fair. But it leaves out the real traffic comparison: with the signal the builder has offered, the intersection stays at C instead of dropping to D.

qualification.reason: The only hedge is a vague 'I'm not going to tell you that number is zero.' There is nothing the commission can check later, such as making approval conditional on the signal that keeps the intersection at C, or the church's written promise to let neighbours park on the lot.

objections.reason: Traffic, the main objection, is answered with 'D isn't gridlock' instead of the signal offer, and several other things the speaker could have used are missing: 20 months of construction trucks on Alder Road, the neighbour parking commitment, and the neighbour group the church has promised to set up.

fit.reason: At about 400 words it fits in three minutes and reads well as spoken testimony, though the name and church are left as placeholders and the closing ask is not the conditional approval the speaker actually wants.
